blocks.title: Photoelectric effect
blocks.text: The photoelectric effect is the emission of electrons from a metal surface exposed to light of suitable frequency or wavelength. The emitted electrons are called photoelectrons.

In the apparatus of Fig 18.1, an evacuated glass tube contains two electrodes. The anode A is joined to the positive terminal of a battery and the metal cathode C to the negative terminal. When monochromatic light of suitable frequency shines on the cathode, it emits electrons, which are attracted to the anode, and the current is measured with a microammeter. The current stops when the light is cut off, showing that it is caused by the light; it is called the photoelectric current.

blocks.alt: Incident light passes through a colour filter onto the photocell X, which holds the cathode C and the anode A. A micro-ammeter A is in series with the cell, a voltmeter V is connected across it, and the cell is fed from the sliding contact of the potential divider Y, which is connected to a battery.
blocks.caption: Figure 18.1: Experimental arrangement to observe photoelectric effect (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 18.1).

blocks.text: To find the maximum energy of the photoelectrons, the battery is reversed, so the anode is negative. The photoelectrons are now repelled and the current falls. At a certain negative voltage, the stopping potential Vo, the current becomes zero: even the most energetic electrons cannot reach the anode. So (1/2) m vmax^2 = Vo e (18.4). With a brighter beam the current is larger but stops at the same Vo (Fig 18.2). With the intensity fixed and different frequencies, the stopping potential is different for each frequency (Fig 18.3), showing that the maximum kinetic energy depends on the frequency.

blocks.alt: A graph of photocurrent Ip against applied voltage, from -V to +V. Two curves, I2 above I1 (I2 > I1), both start from zero current at the same stopping potential Vo on the negative side and level off at different saturation currents.
blocks.caption: Figure 18.2: Characteristic curves of photocurrent vs. applied voltage for two intensities of monochromatic light (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 18.2).

blocks.alt: A graph of photocurrent Ip against applied voltage. The curve for frequency f2 starts from zero at a larger negative voltage than the curve for f1 (f2 > f1); both rise and join at the same saturation current for positive voltage.
blocks.caption: Figure 18.3: Characteristic curves of photocurrent vs applied voltage for light of different frequencies (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 18.3).

items: The electrons are emitted with different energies; their maximum energy depends on the metal and on the frequency of the light, not on its intensity.

There is a minimum frequency, the threshold frequency fo, below which no electrons are emitted, however intense the light. For example, blue light causes photoelectric emission from sodium but red light does not (Fig 18.4). The threshold frequency varies from metal to metal; the corresponding wavelength is the threshold wavelength.
Electrons are emitted instantly; the intensity of the light decides only their number.

blocks.alt: Two wavy light rays. A red ray with a long wavelength, labelled red light (low intensity), ends at 'No electron emitted'. A blue ray with a short wavelength, labelled blue light (high intensity), ends at 'Electron emitted (more electrons)'.
blocks.caption: Figure 18.4: Red and blue light incident on sodium metal (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 18.4).

blocks.text: These results cannot be explained by the electromagnetic wave theory of light. On that theory, increasing the intensity should increase the kinetic energy of the emitted electrons, which contradicts experiment; and even light of low frequency should eventually transfer enough energy to free electrons, which does not happen.
Explanation on the basis of quantum theory

Einstein extended Planck's idea: light is emitted or absorbed in quanta called photons, each of energy E = hf. A photon is absorbed by a single electron in the metal surface. The electron needs a certain minimum energy, the work function phi, to escape from the metal. If the photon energy is enough, the electron is ejected instantly; part of the photon energy frees the electron and the rest becomes its kinetic energy: incident photon energy - work function = (K.E.)max of the photoelectron, or hf - phi = (1/2) m vmax^2 (18.5). This is Einstein's photoelectric equation.

When (K.E.)max is zero, f equals the threshold frequency fo, so hfo - phi = 0, or phi = hfo (18.6). Einstein's equation can also be written (K.E.)max = hf - hfo (18.7). Not every emitted electron has the maximum kinetic energy: some come straight out of the surface while others lose energy in collisions first, and equation 18.7 applies only to those that leave with the full surplus energy. A graph of (K.E.)max against frequency is a straight line of slope h that starts at fo; below fo no emission occurs. Einstein received the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics for explaining the photoelectric effect. The effect cannot be explained if light is a wave with energy spread evenly over its wavefront; it shows the particle nature of light.

blocks.alt: A graph of K.E.max of photoelectrons against light frequency f. A straight line meets the f-axis at the threshold frequency fo and rises to the right; below the axis it is continued as a dashed line back to the K.E.max axis.
blocks.caption: For your information: A graph of the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons vs. light frequency. Below a certain frequency fo, no photoemission occurs (original drawing after the textbook's For your information graph).

blocks.text: Find the energy in eV of a photon of blue light of wavelength 450 nm. Solution: E = hf = hc/lambda = (6.63 x 10^-34 J s)(3 x 10^8 m s^-1)/(450 x 10^-9 m) = 4.42 x 10^-19 J. Since 1 eV = 1.6 x 10^-19 J, E = 4.42 x 10^-19 / 1.6 x 10^-19 = 2.76 eV.

Yellow light of wavelength 577 nm falls on a caesium surface and the stopping voltage is 0.25 V. Find (a) the maximum K.E. of the photoelectrons and (b) the work function of caesium. Solution: (a) (K.E.)max = Vo e = 0.25 V x 1.6 x 10^-19 C = 4 x 10^-20 J = 0.25 eV. (b) phi = hc/lambda - (K.E.)max = (6.63 x 10^-34 x 3 x 10^8)/(577 x 10^-9) - 4 x 10^-20 = 3.45 x 10^-19 J - 0.40 x 10^-19 J = 3.05 x 10^-19 J, which is 1.9 eV.

blocks.title: For your information
blocks.text: How electromagnetic radiation interacts with matter depends on the photon energy: at low energies (below about 0.5 MeV) the photoelectric effect dominates; at intermediate energies the Compton effect dominates; at higher energies (above about 1.2 MeV) pair production dominates.
